title: Not even the reserve bank knows what billions of dollars in banknotes are being used for

(ABC News: Ben Spraggon)

Cash is used for less than one in five transactions, and yet the appetite for new banknotes is only growing.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) has been printing billions of dollars' worth of bills, year after year, for decades.

It's pretty unusual to come across a $100 note in everyday life, so what are they being used for?

There is no shortage of hypotheses, from stacks of cash hidden in suburban households to large-scale illicit activities, but little in the way of definitive answers.

Once they roll off the printing press and flow into the economy, there's no reliable way to track where they end up.

The RBA has been doing its own research into the situation.

Note: These are rough estimates with a large degree of uncertainty; cash is, by its nature, hard to trace.

Let's kick off with the uncontroversial bits. Australians often use cash for everyday transactions, such as at the grocery store.

The RBA's best estimates were that between 9 and 14 per cent of Australia's banknotes are being used for legitimate transactions.

Similarly, between 5 and 9 per cent of banknotes are believed to be lost, forgotten or destroyed.

When it comes to how many banknotes are stashed under grandma's pillow, things become less clear-cut.

The RBA has two ways of estimating how much cash is hoarded by individual households.

The first approach takes advantage of its policy of reimbursing people for damaged banknotes.

By looking at every claim involving damage from residential fires, the central bank's analysts estimated how much cash, on average, households had hoarded at the time their house caught on fire.

The result: 2 per cent of Australia's cash was hoarded domestically.

Next, they tried using data from consumer surveys.

This was self-reported data, from a sample of regular people, asking how much cash they had at home.

The result: 7 to 15 per cent was hoarded domestically.

People aren't likely to say if they have a fortune hidden in the attic, so this is probably still an underestimate.

There is also likely some amount of money hoarded outside of Australia.

The RBA calculates this by looking at overseas shipments of banknotes and then subtracting the cash that tourists bring back into the country.

Again, with a healthy dose of uncertainty, the RBA estimated between zero and 20 per cent is being hoarded internationally.

Finally, there is some amount of cash that is used in the shadow economy.

This could be unreported cash jobs or the proceeds of illegal activities, like producing and selling drugs.

The RBA estimated that this accounted for between 7 and 11 per cent of all banknotes in circulation.

The problem? Even if we take the highest estimate for each category, they only add up to about 70 per cent of the total amount of cash in circulation.

That leaves $32 billion worth of banknotes unaccounted-for.

"It's a mystery," Louis de Koker, a leading expert in money laundering at La Trobe University, says.

"Researchers have theories, but they are still scratching their heads."

The RBA's solution to this mystery is to assume the rest of it is being hoarded, either domestically or internationally.

But why? And by whom? Australia's central bank offers no answers.

A spokesperson from the RBA declined to comment.

We spoke to several experts to investigate their theories about where billions of dollars' worth of banknotes might be hiding.

There are two possibilities for where all this excess cash could be hoarded: in Australian households or overseas.

Some currencies are hoarded outside their respective borders at surprisingly high rates.

According to a recent study from the European Central Bank, more than half of the euro banknotes in circulation are outside the eurozone.

Could the same apply to the Australian dollar?

"The euro is a better-known currency than the Australian dollar," John Hawkins, a former senior economist with the RBA, says.

Outside of Australia, there are only a few Pacific Islands that see widespread usage of the Australian dollar, he says.

If it's not largely hiding out overseas, the bulk of the missing $32 billion must be hoarded by Australian households.

But the maths doesn't quite work out there either.

That would mean an average of about $3,000 per household, a figure that is clearly out of reach for many.

"A staggering amount of the population can't afford an unusual dental bill," Richard Holden, an economist at UNSW, says.

"They're not going to be hoarding thousands of dollars each."

In theory, it's possible that a small number of households are skewing the numbers by hoarding massive quantities of cash. The RBA suggests as much in its analysis.

But to make up the $32 billion shortfall this way, 320,000 households would need to be hoarding $100,000 each. Or is it that 100,000 households have $320,000 squirrelled away for a rainy day?

"Hoarding seems to be part of the answer, but it seems unlikely to provide the full explanation," Professor de Koker says.

This leaves "many uncomfortable questions", he says, about what this massive amount of cash is being used for, and by whom.

There is another possibility for where all the unaccounted-for cash is hiding out.

A forensic look at the data behind the RBA's estimates opens up the possibility that far more of it is being used in criminal enterprises.

For one, the central bank's analysis uses outdated figures to calculate the size of the criminal economy.

The RBA relied on estimates from a 2017 government taskforce report, which suggested Australia's illicit economy may have doubled in size since 2012, even after taking the increase in Australia's overall economy into account.

It then assumes "the share of the economy devoted to underground and illicit activities, as well as the proportion of such activities that are facilitated by cash, has remained unchanged over time" since that 2017 report.

This stretches credulity. Why would the shadow economy double in size over five years, and then flatline for seven immediately after that?

Wastewater monitoring over that period indicates that consumption of many illegal substances is increasing. Cocaine use has more than doubled since 2017.

The RBA's analysts did look at these wastewater measurements, and estimated that the size of Australia's drug economy was $14 billion in 2022/23.

They then reduced this figure down by a factor of almost 10 to $1.6 billion to account for the fact that while individual banknotes will be used multiple times in a single day, others sit in someone's wallet, unspent for months on end.

This means that cash is being transacted at a certain "velocity" in the economy.

The RBA's analysis found the average banknote is re-used about 10 times before returning to the bank (where it can be measured), and that's why the $14 billion drug economy was estimated to hold only $1.6 billion in cold hard cash.

But this velocity figure of about 10 came from the legitimate economy, not the shadow one – and that could be significant.

Dirty money is likely to move "slower" through the economy, says Professor Holden, which would mean the "velocity" factor would really be lower for criminal cash.

This would mean the total value of banknotes held by criminals could be much higher than previously thought.

Another assumption built into the RBA's calculations is that only 2 per cent of the proceeds of drug sales are held as cash.

That's because the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC) reported the seizure of $1.4 billion worth of drugs, and $24 million in cash and other assets in 2021/22.

That's 2 per cent as much cash as drugs.

But there are other ways of interpreting this. Maybe Australia's authorities are good at intercepting drugs, but not so hot at confiscating the cash used to buy them.

When someone purchases drugs with cash, it doesn't just disappear. Dealers and distributors can't easily deposit massive stacks of banknotes at their local bank branch.

It needs to be laundered through the legal economy, used in small increments for everyday purchases or smuggled overseas.

Criminals in the Netherlands in the mid-2000s were sometimes caught smuggling huge volumes of cash across the Atlantic Ocean to pay their suppliers in Colombia.

The smugglers filled backpacks with between 200,000 and 400,000 euros at a time, using exclusively high-denomination bills.

Cash has not lost its allure to money launderers and smugglers in the years since.

Australia's money laundering regulator AUSTRAC still considers cash to be a "mainstay" of money laundering in Australia and abroad.

"Domestically, it is one of the most commonly restrained, forfeited or frozen asset types in criminal asset confiscation matters," the regulator wrote in a 2024 report.

This is particularly true of the largest denominations, as it is unwieldy to stash or transport stacks of $20 bills.

In Australia and around the world, experts have suggested phasing out high-denomination bills for this exact reason. It would make money laundering and smuggling more difficult and expensive.

This has already happened for larger denominations, including the 500 euro note and $10,000 Singaporean note. Both are still legal tender, but new bills are no longer printed.

Still, billions of dollars in drug money are slipping through cracks in Australia's anti-money laundering efforts every year.

There is no doubt that there are massive stacks of cash, mostly in large denominations, out there somewhere. These hidden stashes could hold more than half of all the banknotes in circulation.

This cash is not being reported in consumer surveys, or claimed back when damaged in house fires.

Whether we call it hoarded or part of the shadow economy, the majority of it is unlikely to be completely clean.
